lab.title: A safe storage sandbox
lab.scenario: Create a small file-backed filesystem, mount it, fill it, inspect it, and clean up. No real disk is touched.

steps.text: Inspect the current storage map and capacity.
steps.verify: Identify which filesystem holds / and what else is mounted.

steps.text: Create a 64 MB file and format it as XFS.
steps.cmd: dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/lab-disk.img bs=1M count=64 status=progress && sudo mkfs.xfs /tmp/lab-disk.img
steps.verify: mkfs refuses if the target already has a filesystem; that is a feature.

steps.text: Mount it on a new directory and inspect the mount.
steps.cmd: sudo mkdir -p /mnt/labdisk && sudo mount -o loop /tmp/lab-disk.img /mnt/labdisk && findmnt /mnt/labdisk
steps.verify: findmnt /mnt/labdisk should show the loop device and XFS filesystem type.

steps.text: Write data, check usage, and calculate directory consumption.
steps.cmd: sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/mnt/labdisk/fill bs=1M count=20 && df -h /mnt/labdisk && du -sh /mnt/labdisk
steps.verify: df should show the new filesystem with used space, and du should report the fill file.

steps.text: Unmount and remove the file-backed disk.

quiz.q: Which command shows filesystem UUIDs and types?
quiz.why: lsblk -f prints filesystem type, label, UUID, and mount point. blkid also queries this information.

quiz.q: df shows free space but writes fail with "No space left on device." What should you check?
quiz.why: A filesystem can exhaust inodes while blocks remain free. df -i reveals it.

quiz.q: Why use a UUID in /etc/fstab instead of /dev/sdb1?
options: Device names can change across boots and hardware changes
quiz.why: Device enumeration order can change. UUIDs identify the filesystem itself, making mounts stable.
